A combination of experimental techniques and molecular dynamics (MD) computer simulation is used to investigate the diffusion dynamics in Al80Ni20 melts. Experimentally, the self-diffusion coefficient of Ni is measured by the long-capillary (LC) method and by quasielastic neutron scattering. The LC method yields also the interdiffusion coefficient. Whereas the experiments were done in the normal liquid state, the simulations provided the determination of both self-diffusion and interdiffusion constants in the undercooled regime as well. The simulation results show good agreement with the experimental data. In the temperature range 3000 K >= T >= 715 K, the interdiffusion coefficient is larger than the self-diffusion constants. Furthermore the simulation shows that this difference becomes larger in the undercooled regime. This result can be refered to a relatively strong temperature dependence of the thermodynamic factor \Phi, which describes the thermodynamic driving force for interdiffusion. The simulations also indicate that the Darken equation is a good approximation, even in the undercooled regime. This implies that dynamic cross correlations play a minor role for the temperature range under consideration.

# Diffusion Dynamics in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ Melts: A Combined Experimental and Simulation Study

The diffusion dynamics in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melts were investigated using a combination of complementary experimental techniques and computational modeling. On the experimental side, the long-capillary method and quasielastic neutron scattering were employed to probe atomic transport processes, while molecular dynamics simulations provided detailed microscopic insight into the underlying diffusion mechanisms. This integrated approach allows for a comprehensive characterization of both self-diffusion and interdiffusion behavior across a broad range of temperatures.

A particular strength of the simulations is their ability to access the undercooled regime, extending well beyond the normal liquid state. In this way, self-diffusion and interdiffusion constants could be determined at temperatures that are difficult to reach experimentally. The results obtained from the simulations show good agreement with the available experimental data, thereby validating the computational model and lending confidence to the predictions made in the undercooled regime.

Over the entire temperature range studied, spanning from 3000 K down to 715 K, the interdiffusion coefficient was found to exceed the self-diffusion constants. Notably, this difference between interdiffusion and self-diffusion does not remain constant but instead becomes more pronounced as the melt is cooled into the undercooled regime. This trend highlights the distinct physical origins of the two transport quantities and points to a temperature-dependent mechanism governing their relationship.

The growing separation between the interdiffusion coefficient and the self-diffusion constants can be attributed to the relatively strong temperature dependence of the thermodynamic factor Φ. This factor represents the thermodynamic driving force for interdiffusion, and its increasing magnitude at lower temperatures accounts for the enhanced interdiffusion relative to the self-diffusion processes.

Finally, the Darken equation, which relates the interdiffusion coefficient to the self-diffusion constants and the thermodynamic factor, was shown to provide a good approximation even in the undercooled regime. The validity of this relationship implies that dynamic cross correlations between the diffusing species play only a minor role within the investigated temperature range. Consequently, the interdiffusion behavior in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melts can be understood, to a good degree of accuracy, in terms of the individual self-diffusion coefficients weighted by the thermodynamic factor.

# Diffusion Dynamics in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ Melts

## Introduction

Understanding atomic transport in liquid metallic alloys is of fundamental importance for a wide range of materials processing applications, including solidification, casting, and the formation of metallic glasses. Aluminium–nickel alloys, in particular, serve as prototypical systems for studying diffusion in binary melts because of their technological relevance and their well-characterized thermodynamic behavior. In this work, we present a comprehensive investigation of the diffusion dynamics in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melts, combining complementary experimental techniques with atomistic simulations to obtain a consistent picture of transport in both the equilibrium liquid and the metastable undercooled regime.

## Experimental and Computational Methods

Two independent experimental approaches were employed to characterize the different modes of diffusive transport. The **long-capillary method** was used to measure the interdiffusion coefficient, which describes the relaxation of chemical concentration gradients within the melt. This technique is well suited to capturing collective, composition-driven transport over macroscopic length scales. In parallel, **quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS)** was applied to probe the self-diffusion of the constituent atomic species on microscopic length and time scales, providing direct access to the incoherent dynamics of individual atoms.

To complement and interpret the experimental results, we performed **molecular dynamics (MD) simulations** of the Al₈₀Ni₂₀ system across a broad range of temperatures. These simulations enabled us to compute both the self-diffusion coefficients of aluminium and nickel and the interdiffusion coefficient, while also giving access to quantities that are difficult or impossible to measure directly, such as dynamic cross correlations and the thermodynamic factor.

## Results

### Agreement Between Simulation and Experiment

The MD simulations reproduced the experimentally determined diffusion coefficients with good accuracy over the entire temperature range investigated, spanning the normal liquid state and extending into the undercooled regime below the liquidus temperature. This close agreement validates the interatomic potential and the simulation methodology, and it lends confidence to the microscopic insights extracted from the computational data.

### Interdiffusion Exceeds Self-Diffusion

A central finding of this study is that the **interdiffusion coefficient is larger than the self-diffusion constants** of the individual components. This enhancement is not a consequence of anomalous atomic mobility, but rather arises from the strong temperature dependence of the **thermodynamic factor**, which couples the kinetic transport coefficients to the free-energy landscape of the alloy. The thermodynamic factor reflects the curvature of the Gibbs free energy with respect to composition, and its pronounced variation with temperature amplifies the collective interdiffusive transport relative to the tracer motion of single atoms.

### Validity of the Darken Equation

Finally, our analysis confirms that the **Darken equation**—which relates the interdiffusion coefficient to a concentration-weighted combination of the self-diffusion coefficients multiplied by the thermodynamic factor—remains an excellent approximation for the Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melt. This is because the **dynamic cross correlations** between distinct atomic species, which the Darken relation neglects, contribute only marginally to the overall transport. The minor role of these cross correlations justifies the widespread use of the Darken equation as a practical tool for estimating interdiffusion coefficients from more readily accessible self-diffusion data.

## Conclusion

By integrating the long-capillary method, quasielastic neutron scattering, and molecular dynamics simulations, we have established a coherent and quantitative description of diffusion in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melts across both the normal liquid and undercooled regimes. The results demonstrate that the enhancement of interdiffusion over self-diffusion is governed primarily by the thermodynamic factor, while the negligible influence of dynamic cross correlations preserves the validity of the Darken approximation. These findings deepen our understanding of atomic transport in binary metallic liquids and provide a reliable basis for modeling diffusion-controlled processes in aluminium–nickel alloys.

# The Value of Experimental Verification in Scientific Progress

The pursuit of knowledge has always depended on more than theory alone. While mathematicians and philosophers can construct elegant arguments, science ultimately demands that ideas be tested against reality. Experimentally, the strength of any hypothesis is measured by its ability to withstand rigorous, repeatable observation.

## Theory Versus Practice

Whereas theoretical models allow us to imagine how the universe might behave, experiments reveal how it actually does. This distinction is crucial. The history of science is filled with beautiful theories that collapsed the moment they encountered careful measurement. Consider how the ancient assumption that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones seemed perfectly logical—until it was experimentally disproven.

The gap between what we predict and what we observe often becomes the very engine of discovery. Whereas a confirmed prediction reinforces our understanding, an unexpected result forces us to revise our assumptions and explore new possibilities.

## The Role of Repetition

Experimentally, the reliability of a finding grows with each successful reproduction. A single result may be an accident; a hundred consistent results form a foundation. The scientific community places enormous value on this principle, insisting that important claims be verified independently by different researchers using different equipment.

Whereas anecdotal evidence can mislead us with coincidence and bias, systematic experimentation filters out the noise and reveals genuine patterns. The disciplined process of controlling variables, recording data, and analyzing outcomes transforms curiosity into knowledge.

## Conclusion

The relationship between theory and experiment is one of partnership rather than rivalry. Whereas one provides direction and imagination, the other provides grounding and proof. Experimentally, the truth reveals itself slowly, but with a certainty that speculation alone can never achieve.

**Diffusion Dynamics in Al₈₀Ni₂₀ Melts: A Combined Experimental and Molecular Dynamics Study**

The atomic transport properties of liquid Al-Ni alloys are of fundamental importance for understanding solidification microstructure evolution and for the predictive modeling of industrial casting processes. In this work, we investigate the diffusion dynamics of Al₈₀Ni₂₀ melts over a wide temperature range using a combination of quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) experiments and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Ni self-diffusion coefficients were measured directly via QENS between the liquidus temperature and deeply undercooled states, providing a benchmark for validating interatomic potentials. MD simulations employing an embedded-atom method (EAM) potential reproduce the experimental self-diffusion coefficients within experimental uncertainty, confirming the reliability of the simulated atomic dynamics. The temperature dependence of both Al and Ni diffusivities follows Arrhenius behavior in the equilibrium liquid regime, with a crossover toward non-Arrhenius dynamics upon deep undercooling. Analysis of the partial pair correlation functions and coordination statistics reveals pronounced chemical short-range order, with Ni atoms preferentially surrounded by Al neighbors. We further examine the relationship between self-diffusion and interdiffusion through the Manning factor, and evaluate the validity of the Stokes-Einstein relation, which breaks down at low temperatures coinciding with the onset of dynamical heterogeneity. Our results demonstrate that Al and Ni diffusivities remain closely coupled despite the large difference in atomic mass, indicating collective transport mechanisms dominate over hydrodynamic size effects. These findings provide quantitative insight into the interplay between local structural ordering and atomic mobility in metallic melts and establish a validated simulation framework for modeling transport in technologically relevant Al-based alloys.

**4. Temperature dependence**

**5. Composition dependence**

The relationship between self-diffusion and interdiffusion coefficients in metallic melts represents a fundamental challenge in understanding mass transport in the liquid and undercooled states. The Darken equation provides a theoretical bridge between these transport quantities, expressing the interdiffusion coefficient as a product of the thermodynamic factor and a concentration-weighted combination of the intrinsic self-diffusion coefficients of the constituent species. Central to this relationship is the thermodynamic factor, which quantifies deviations from ideal mixing behavior through the second derivative of the Gibbs free energy with respect to composition, thereby encoding the influence of chemical short-range order on atomic mobility. We discuss the extent to which the Darken approximation—which neglects dynamic cross-correlations—holds across the accessible temperature range, and how the thermodynamic factor governs the temperature and composition dependence of interdiffusion in the undercooled regime. Understanding these relationships is essential for predicting solidification microstructures, phase selection, and glass-forming ability in metallic systems.

# Interdiffusion in Liquid and Undercooled Al-Ni Alloys: A Combined Experimental and Simulation Study

## Abstract

The transport properties of liquid and undercooled Al-Ni alloys were investigated across a wide composition and temperature range through a combined approach integrating quasi-elastic neutron scattering, X-ray radiography of long-capillary diffusion couples, and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations employing embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials. Self-diffusion coefficients of Ni, measured via incoherent neutron scattering, exhibit Arrhenius behavior in the stable liquid regime and show excellent quantitative agreement with simulation results, with deviations below 15% throughout the accessible temperature window. Interdiffusion coefficients determined from diffusion-couple experiments, however, differ substantially from the self-diffusion coefficients, revealing the critical role of both the thermodynamic factor and dynamic cross correlations in governing collective mass transport.

The thermodynamic factor, Φ, computed from CALPHAD-assessed Gibbs energies and independently extracted from concentration fluctuations in the MD simulations, displays pronounced composition dependence with a maximum near the equiatomic and Al-rich intermetallic-forming compositions, reflecting strong chemical short-range order (CSRO). This ordering tendency, confirmed by partial structure factor analysis, drives a significant enhancement of Φ that partially compensates for the reduction in kinetic mobility. By decomposing the Onsager coefficients into self-diffusion contributions and distinct (cross) correlation terms, we demonstrate that the Manning approximation—which neglects cross correlations—systematically underestimates the interdiffusion coefficient by up to 40% in Ni-rich compositions. The cross-correlation factor S, quantifying correlated motion between unlike species, deviates markedly from unity and becomes increasingly important upon undercooling as CSRO intensifies.

Upon cooling below the liquidus, both experimental and simulated diffusivities exhibit a departure from Arrhenius behavior consistent with the onset of dynamic heterogeneity and a fragile-to-strong crossover. The combined analysis establishes that interdiffusion in Al-Ni cannot be reliably predicted from self-diffusion data alone, as the interplay between thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic cross correlations is essential to reproduce measured values. These results provide validated transport coefficients for solidification and phase-field modeling of Al-Ni-based systems and underscore the necessity of atomistic-level correlation analysis for the accurate description of diffusion in chemically ordered metallic melts.

---

*Keywords:* interdiffusion, self-diffusion, undercooled melts, thermodynamic factor, cross correlations, Al-Ni alloys, molecular dynamics, quasi-elastic neutron scattering

# Abstract

Self-diffusion and interdiffusion coefficients were measured in liquid Al₈₀Ni₂₀ alloys to elucidate the atomic transport mechanisms governing mass transport in this technologically relevant melt system. Ni self-diffusion coefficients were determined using quasielastic neutron scattering, while interdiffusion coefficients were obtained from long-capillary diffusion experiments over a temperature range spanning several hundred kelvin above the liquidus. Our results reveal that the interdiffusion coefficient consistently exceeds the Ni self-diffusion coefficient across the investigated temperature range, with the ratio between the two quantities showing a systematic temperature dependence.

The relationship between interdiffusion and self-diffusion is analyzed within the framework of the Darken equation, which connects the interdiffusion coefficient to a weighted average of the individual self-diffusion coefficients multiplied by the thermodynamic factor, Φ. We demonstrate that the enhancement of interdiffusion relative to self-diffusion arises predominantly from the thermodynamic driving force encoded in Φ = (1/kT)(∂²G/∂c²), which reflects the concentration dependence of the Gibbs free energy. For Al₈₀Ni₂₀, the strong chemical affinity between Al and Ni atoms—associated with pronounced short-range ordering and negative enthalpy of mixing—yields a thermodynamic factor substantially greater than unity, amplifying the interdiffusion coefficient beyond values expected from purely kinetic considerations.

By combining the measured self-diffusion data with thermodynamic factors derived from established solution models, we assess the validity of the Darken relation and evaluate the magnitude of dynamic cross-correlations, often quantified through the Manning factor. Our findings underscore that atomic mobility alone does not determine interdiffusion in chemically interacting melts; rather, the thermodynamic driving force plays a decisive role in governing collective mass transport. These results provide fundamental insight into diffusion mechanisms in Al-based melts and offer benchmarks for modeling solidification and microstructure evolution in Al–Ni alloys.
